title: VAMP-Diff: VampPrior Latent Diffusion for Photoplethysmography Modeling

paper.title:
VAMP-Diff: VampPrior Latent Diffusion
for Photoplethysmography Modeling Thanks: Code at: https://github.com/fatighasemi74/VAMP-Diff
paper.abstract: Abstract Photoplethysmography (PPG) has become a ubiquitous physiological signal; however, current generative models still struggle to preserve realistic waveform morphology and learn a latent structure that captures cardiac and respiratory physiology. PPG generators trained with adversarial losses can produce plausible waveforms, but provide no inference path from a real signal to a latent representation. Variational autoencoders, on the other hand, map the PPG data to latent codes, although their decoders often blur systolic upstrokes and dampen amplitude and spectral details. Diffusion models improve waveform fidelity, but typically lack an inference path for reconstruction and physiological analysis. We propose VampPrior Latent Diffusion (VAMP-Diff), a jointly trained variational diffusion model that combines a temporal PPG encoder, a conditional one-dimensional diffusion decoder, and VampPrior regularization on a compact pooled latent. The model uses full temporal latent during diffusion reconstruction, giving the decoder access to beat timing and morphology, while generating samples from learned VampPrior components instead of a fixed Gaussian prior. We demonstrate on the CapnoBase dataset that VAMP-Diff produces realistic PPG signals, reconstructs sharper physiological waveforms than Gaussian-prior baselines, preserves heart-rate information, maintains respiratory-rate consistency, and is sensitive to waveform corruptions through reconstruction error.

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Photoplethysmography (PPG) [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] is a non-invasive optical technique that encodes cardiac and respiratory physiology in a periodic waveform. Generative modeling of PPG requires preserving both global structure, such as dominant periodicity and amplitude, and local morphology, such as the systolic upstroke, dicrotic notch, and inter-beat variation. This is a challenging task since clinically relevant information in PPG signals is distributed across multiple timescales: cardiac periodicity at 0.7 0.7 – 3.0 3.0 Hz, respiratory modulation at 0.1 0.1 – 0.5 0.5 Hz, and beat-level morphological features that occur within individual cycles. A generative model that collapses this temporal structure into a single latent vector loses the positional information needed to reconstruct these features faithfully. The scarcity of large labeled PPG datasets motivates the need for generative models that produce physiologically realistic synthetic signals for downstream tasks such as respiratory rate estimation [ 4 , 5 ] . Generative approaches for PPG and related physiological signals include generative adversarial networks (GANs) [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] that optimize adversarial objectives to match signal statistics and diffusion models [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] that model the full conditional distribution through iterative denoising. Latent diffusion models [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] combine a learned latent space with a diffusion decoder but train the two components separately. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) [ 17 ] learn structured latent representations, and hierarchical VAEs [ 18 , 19 ] have demonstrated strong performance on image generation. Diffusion priors have also been introduced into VAEs to improve generation [ 20 , 21 ] , Recent work has also combined the VampPrior [ 22 ] with hierarchical VAEs to improve prior expressiveness [ 23 ] ; however, this occurs in a setting different from one-dimensional physiological signal generation. None of these approaches jointly trains a temporal encoder and a diffusion decoder under a data-adaptive prior. Without joint training, the latent space cannot adapt to both the KL regularization and the decoder’s reconstruction objective simultaneously, which limits the fidelity of generated waveforms and their utility for physiological inference. We propose VAMP-Diff, a jointly trained variational diffusion model that combines a temporal PPG encoder, a conditional one-dimensional diffusion decoder, and a VampPrior defined on a compact pooled latent, evaluated on CapnoBase [ 24 ] . We also introduce a morphology-preserving loss that supplements the variational diffusion objective with spectral, derivative, amplitude, and peak-to-peak terms to enforce waveform fidelity beyond sample-level error. VAMP-Diff reconstructs sharper physiological waveforms than Gaussian-prior baselines, preserves heart-rate information, and maintains respiratory-rate estimator consistency on held-out test signals. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II provides background on PPG, VAEs, and diffusion models. Section III describes the proposed model and training objective. Section IV defines downstream evaluation tasks, and Section V reports empirical results. Finally, concluding remarks are provided in Section VI .

sections.heading: II-A Photoplethysmography
sections.text: Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a non-invasive optical technique that measures pulsatile changes in blood volume in peripheral tissue, producing a periodic waveform that encodes heart rate, respiratory rate, and autonomic activity [ 1 , 2 ] . Since PPG sensors are inexpensive and easy to deploy, they are widely used in clinical monitors and wearable devices, with applications that range from cardiovascular monitoring to biometric analysis [ 25 , 26 ] . However, PPG waveforms are difficult to model since clinically relevant information is distributed across peak timing, systolic upstroke, dicrotic morphology, amplitude changes, and slower respiratory variation across the window. Large labeled PPG datasets are also hard to obtain because data collection often requires controlled acquisition, expert annotation, and privacy protection under regulations such as HIPAA, which leaves only a small number of public datasets such as CapnoBase and related physiological signal resources [ 24 , 27 , 25 , 26 ] .

sections.heading: III-E Architecture of VAMP-Diff
sections.text: VAMP-Diff combines latent inference, prior learning, and waveform synthesis in a single jointly trained architecture. Given an observed PPG window x 0 x_{0} , the encoder outputs posterior parameters μ ϕ ​ ( x 0 ) \mu_{\phi}(x_{0}) and σ ϕ 2 ​ ( x 0 ) \sigma_{\phi}^{2}(x_{0}) for the full temporal latent z ∈ ℝ C z × T z z\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{z}\times T_{z}} , which conditions the diffusion decoder. The learnable pseudo-inputs { u k } k = 1 K \{u_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} pass through the same encoder to form the VampPrior components used during training and generation. Figure 1 shows the shared encoder structure and the distinction between the full latent z z and the pooled latent z ~ = A ​ z \widetilde{z}=Az . The KL comparison only utilizes the pooled latent z ~ = A ​ z ∈ ℝ C z × T c \widetilde{z}=Az\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{z}\times T_{c}} ; the decoder receives the full temporal latent, which preserves temporal order through the diffusion updates. The conditional one-dimensional U-Net predicts x ^ 0 = f θ ​ ( x t , t , z ) \widehat{x}_{0}=f_{\theta}(x_{t},t,z) , and the decoder blocks receive z z through multiscale FiLM modulation. This architecture keeps the KL computation tractable by applying prior matching only to the pooled latent. The diffusion decoder still receives the full temporal latent for reconstruction and generation, and the encoder, pseudo-inputs, and diffusion decoder are optimized jointly using the loss function ( 11 ). sections.heading: IV Downstream Tasks
sections.text: We evaluate downstream behavior using reconstructed test signals to determine whether the learned latent representation preserves physiological content from the original PPG window. For each test signal x 0 x_{0} , the encoder produces z = μ ϕ ​ ( x 0 ) z=\mu_{\phi}(x_{0}) , and the decoder reconstructs x ^ 0 \widehat{x}_{0} through deterministic DDIM with η = 0 \eta=0 , as described in Section III-B . Both x 0 x_{0} and x ^ 0 \widehat{x}_{0} are denormalized with the training-set statistics μ train \mu_{\mathrm{train}} and σ train \sigma_{\mathrm{train}} . This process evaluates the encoder and decoder jointly, since the latent must keep a physiologically relevant structure and the diffusion decoder must recover that structure through the denoising process. We consider three test-split evaluations, heart-rate estimation, respiratory-rate estimator consistency, and reconstruction-based waveform corruption detection.

sections.heading: IV-A Heart-Rate Estimation
sections.text: Heart rate (HR) estimation is the first physiological test for PPG, as cardiac rhythm is the dominant periodic component of clean PPG, and accurate recovery depends primarily on inter-beat timing rather than pointwise waveform similarity [ 2 , 3 ] . For each test window, both x 0 x_{0} and x ^ 0 \widehat{x}_{0} are bandpass-filtered to 0.7 0.7 – 3.0 3.0 Hz before cardiac feature extraction. Systolic peaks are detected with minimum inter-peak distance 0.35 0.35 s, prominence 0.1 ​ σ 0.1\sigma of the filtered signal, and height at the 60 60 th percentile. Per-window HR is computed as 60 / IBI ¯ 60/\bar{\mathrm{IBI}} , where IBI ¯ \bar{\mathrm{IBI}} is the mean inter-beat interval. Signal-level reconstruction is evaluated using MAE, RMSE, and Pearson correlation. Cardiac timing fidelity is assessed through HR absolute error and IBI mean absolute error on the VAMP-Diff model.

sections.heading: IV-B Respiratory Rate Estimation
sections.text: Respiratory rate (RR) is a more demanding physiological test, since respiration affects PPG through baseline variation, amplitude modulation, and frequency modulation in the 0.1 0.1 – 0.5 0.5 Hz band [ 3 ] . We use a frozen-estimator procedure so that RR evaluation stays independent of VAMP-Diff training. A one-dimensional ResNet is trained once on real PPG to regress RR from CO 2 -derived labels, and the generative model is not used during estimator training. The estimator uses a stride-2 stem with kernel size 11 11 and 32 32 channels, followed by four residual stages with channel widths { 32 , 64 , 128 , 128 } \{32,64,128,128\} , dilation rates { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \{1,2,4,8\} , global average pooling, and a two-layer MLP regression head. Ground-truth RR is obtained from the synchronous EtCO 2 channel in CapnoBase [ 24 ] by peak detection on a five-sample-smoothed signal, with minimum inter-peak distance 1 1 s and prominence 0.05 0.05 . Recordings outside [ 6 , 35 ] [6,35] breaths per minute are excluded. We apply the frozen estimator to real and reconstructed PPG windows, and use MAE recon − MAE real \mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{recon}}-\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{real}} to measure how much RR-relevant information changes after reconstruction.

sections.heading: V Empirical Results
sections.text: The proposed VAMP-Diff model is evaluated along two axes: generative quality and reconstruction fidelity, validated through model comparison and downstream physiological inference tasks. The former tests whether the model produces PPG signals that are statistically and morphologically consistent with real data; the latter tests whether the encoded latent z z carries sufficient physiological information to recover clinically meaningful quantities through the decode pipeline, as measured by the downstream tasks of Section IV .

sections.heading: V-A Dataset and Preprocessing
sections.text: Experiments use the CapnoBase dataset [ 24 ] , a freely available ICU recording containing PPG and capnography signals from 42 patients, each recorded for approximately 8 minutes at 300 Hz. The PPG channel ( pleth_y ) provides the input signal. Respiratory-rate ground truth is derived from the synchronous EtCO 2 channel ( CO 2 _y ) as described in Section IV-B . Each recording is segmented into overlapping windows of 3,072 3{,}072 samples ( 10.24 10.24 s). A bandpass filter ( 0.7 0.7 – 3.0 3.0 Hz) is applied transiently for peak-based quality checking only; windows with fewer than two detected systolic peaks are discarded. The stored windows retain the full signal spectrum, including the respiratory modulation band ( 0.1 0.1 – 0.5 0.5 Hz), which is necessary for downstream respiratory rate estimation. Windows are normalized using the training-set mean μ train \mu_{\text{train}} and the standard deviation σ train \sigma_{\text{train}} , retained for denormalization at evaluation. The dataset yields 6,815 6{,}815 training, 1,410 1{,}410 validation, and 1,645 1{,}645 test windows. Recordings are split at the patient level, ensuring that no patient appears in more than one split and preventing data leakage between training and evaluation.

sections.heading: V-B Implementation Details
sections.text: Architecture details are described in Section III . The encoder and decoder are trained jointly after a 20-epoch freeze phase that allows the decoder and pseudo-inputs to stabilize before the encoder is updated. Separate learning rates are used for each component because they play different roles: the pseudo-inputs require a higher rate to track the changing posterior, while the encoder uses a lower rate to avoid destabilizing the latent space. The KL weight β \beta is annealed rather than fixed to prevent posterior collapse early in training. sections.heading: V-C Empirical Result 1: Model Comparison
sections.text: To highlight the benefits of the proposed design, we compare our model to a Vanilla VAE with a similar encoder architecture and a normal Gaussian, and the proposed VAE-Diff model with a normal Gaussian prior.

sections.heading: V-C 1 Reconstruction Quality
sections.text: In Table II , compares reconstruction quality across three models. VAMP-Diff achieves comparable pointwise reconstruction to VAE-Diff while reducing HR absolute error. The Vanilla VAE produces the lowest pointwise error but the highest HR reconstruction error ( 3.5 3.5 bpm), since its decoder averages over the conditional distribution and blurs peak timing. HR reconstruction error decreases sharply when the decoder is swapped for the diffusion model (a 77% reduction, from 3.5 → 0.8 3.5\rightarrow 0.8 bpm), meaning that the diffusion decoder preserves temporal periodicity much better because it learns the full conditional distribution, not just the mean. Adding the VampPrior further reduces HR error ( 0.8 → 0.556 0.8\rightarrow 0.556 bpm). This supports the claim that the VampPrior regularizes the posterior toward a more structured prior, encouraging the encoder to represent temporal periodicity more accurately. Figure 2 shows representative reconstructions from all three models on the same test window. Unconditional generation reveals a more fundamental difference between models. When sampling from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) , the Gaussian prior does not match the aggregate posterior learned by the encoder, so generation-time samples fall outside the latent regions seen during training. The VampPrior addresses this by adapting the prior to the encoder’s aggregate posterior, enabling VAMP-Diff to produce realistic PPG unconditionally shown in Figure 3 . sections.text: Table III isolates the contribution of each design choice. sections.heading: VI Conclusions
sections.text: This paper presented VAMP-Diff, a jointly trained variational diffusion model for PPG signal modeling that combines a temporal encoder, a conditional one-dimensional diffusion decoder, and a VampPrior regularizer on a compact pooled latent. The model passes the full temporal latent to the decoder during reconstruction and generation, and hence beat timing, pulse morphology, amplitude structure, and respiratory modulation stay available to the denoising process, and the compact VampPrior KL makes prior matching tractable without forcing generation through a fixed Gaussian prior. Experiments on CapnoBase show that VAMP-Diff generates physiologically realistic PPG waveforms, improves heart-rate preservation over Gaussian-prior baselines, maintains respiratory-rate estimator consistency, and shows reconstruction-error sensitivity to waveform corruptions.

sections.heading: Appendix B Waveform Corruption Detection
sections.text: CapnoBase does not provide annotated abnormal PPG events. To check whether reconstruction error is sensitive to abnormal waveform structure, we use synthetic waveform corruptions as a sanity check with reconstruction error, and not as a standalone anomaly benchmark. Clean test windows are corrupted with additive Gaussian noise, low-frequency baseline wander, amplitude clipping, and partial flatline. These corruptions represent broadband noise, slow drift, dynamic-range saturation, and signal dropout. The trained model is applied to clean and corrupted windows without anomaly-specific training, and per-window reconstruction error is used as the anomaly score. This experiment checks whether deviations from the learned clean PPG distribution receive larger reconstruction errors. We report AUROC, AUPRC, TPR@ 5 % 5\% FPR, and the Spearman correlation between scores computed on input signals and scores computed on reconstructions.

sections.heading: B-A Empirical Results: Anomaly Detection Sanity Check
sections.text: As a sanity check on whether reconstruction error reflects signal quality, anomalous windows are constructed by injecting four types of synthetic corruption into random subset of the 1,645 1{,}645 clean test windows. Each corruption type is applied to an equal share of the subset: 136 136 windows receive additive Gaussian noise (motion artifact), 136 136 receive slow baseline wander (breathing artifact), 135 135 receive amplitude clipping (sensor saturation), and 135 135 receive partial flatline (signal loss), yielding 542 542 anomalous windows in total. The remaining 1,645 1{,}645 windows are kept clean and treated as normal, giving a final evaluation set of 2,187 2{,}187 windows with a 75.2 % 75.2\% / 24.8 % 24.8\% normal/anomalous split. Two anomaly scores are computed from each encode-decode pass: the mean absolute error MAE ⁡ ( x 0 , x ^ 0 ) \mathrm{MAE}(x_{0},\hat{x}_{0}) and the correlation-based score 1 − ρ 1-\rho , where ρ \rho is the Pearson correlation between input and reconstruction. No anomaly-specific training is performed; the model was trained exclusively on clean signals, so corrupted inputs that fall outside the learned latent distribution are expected to produce higher reconstruction error. Results are mixed and corruption-dependent, as shown in Table IX . Gaussian noise is detected perfectly (AUROC = 1.0 =1.0 , MAE anomalous = 0.593 {}_{\text{anomalous}}=0.593 vs MAE normal = 0.039 {}_{\text{normal}}=0.039 ), because high-frequency random corruption falls entirely outside the smooth periodic structure of the learned latent space. Baseline wander is partially separated (AUROC = 0.847 =0.847 ). Amplitude clipping performs below chance (AUROC = 0.400 =0.400 ) because clipped signals retain regular periodicity and are reconstructed faithfully as low-amplitude PPG, so the model cannot distinguish them from genuinely low-amplitude normal signals. The overall AUROC of 0.739 0.739 should be interpreted cautiously given the poor clipping result; the Spearman correlation r = 0.98 r=0.98 between input and reconstruction anomaly scores confirms the pipeline preserves signal quality ordering, but this experiment is not intended as a standalone anomaly detection benchmark. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2605.22851v1 [eess.SP] 17 May 2026 VAMP-Diff: VampPrior Latent Diffusion for Photoplethysmography Modeling Thanks: Code at: https://github.com/fatighasemi74/VAMP-Diff Fatemeh Ghasemi Balouei 1 Nathan Willemsen 2 Mahesh Banavar 1 Bahman Moraffah 3 Affiliation: 1 Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Clarkson University, Potsdam, USA 2 Data Science, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, USA 3 Department of Computer Science, Data Science, and Artificial Intelligence, Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, USA {ghasemf, mbanavar}@clarkson.edu {nawillemsen, bmoraffah}@wpi.edu Abstract Photoplethysmography (PPG) has become a ubiquitous physiological signal; however, current generative models still struggle to preserve realistic waveform morphology and learn a latent structure that captures cardiac and respiratory physiology. PPG generators trained with adversarial losses can produce plausible waveforms, but provide no inference path from a real signal to a latent representation. Variational autoencoders, on the other hand, map the PPG data to latent codes, although their decoders often blur systolic upstrokes and dampen amplitude and spectral details. Diffusion models improve waveform fidelity, but typically lack an inference path for reconstruction and physiological analysis. We propose VampPrior Latent Diffusion (VAMP-Diff), a jointly trained variational diffusion model that combines a temporal PPG encoder, a conditional one-dimensional diffusion decoder, and VampPrior regularization on a compact pooled latent. The model uses full temporal latent during diffusion reconstruction, giving the decoder access to beat timing and morphology, while generating samples from learned VampPrior components instead of a fixed Gaussian prior. We demonstrate on the CapnoBase dataset that VAMP-Diff produces realistic PPG signals, reconstructs sharper physiological waveforms than Gaussian-prior baselines, preserves heart-rate information, maintains respiratory-rate consistency, and is sensitive to waveform corruptions through reconstruction error. I Introduction Photoplethysmography (PPG) [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] is a non-invasive optical technique that encodes cardiac and respiratory physiology in a periodic waveform. Generative modeling of PPG requires preserving both global structure, such as dominant periodicity and amplitude, and local morphology, such as the systolic upstroke, dicrotic notch, and inter-beat variation. This is a challenging task since clinically relevant information in PPG signals is distributed across multiple timescales: cardiac periodicity at 0.7 0.7 – 3.0 3.0 Hz, respiratory modulation at 0.1 0.1 – 0.5 0.5 Hz, and beat-level morphological features that occur within individual cycles. A generative model that collapses this temporal structure into a single latent vector loses the positional information needed to reconstruct these features faithfully. The scarcity of large labeled PPG datasets motivates the need for generative models that produce physiologically realistic synthetic signals for downstream tasks such as respiratory rate estimation [ 4 , 5 ] . Generative approaches for PPG and related physiological signals include generative adversarial networks (GANs) [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] that optimize adversarial objectives to match signal statistics and diffusion models [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] that model the full conditional distribution through iterative denoising. Latent diffusion models [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] combine a learned latent space with a diffusion decoder but train the two components separately. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) [ 17 ] learn structured latent representations, and hierarchical VAEs [ 18 , 19 ] have demonstrated strong performance on image generation. Diffusion priors have also been introduced into VAEs to improve generation [ 20 , 21 ] , Recent work has also combined the VampPrior [ 22 ] with hierarchical VAEs to improve prior expressiveness [ 23 ] ; however, this occurs in a setting different from one-dimensional physiological signal generation. None of these approaches jointly trains a temporal encoder and a diffusion decoder under a data-adaptive prior. Without joint training, the latent space cannot adapt to both the KL regularization and the decoder’s reconstruction objective simultaneously, which limits the fidelity of generated waveforms and their utility for physiological inference. We propose VAMP-Diff, a jointly trained variational diffusion model that combines a temporal PPG encoder, a conditional one-dimensional diffusion decoder, and a VampPrior defined on a compact pooled latent, evaluated on CapnoBase [ 24 ] . We also introduce a morphology-preserving loss that supplements the variational diffusion objective with spectral, derivative, amplitude, and peak-to-peak terms to enforce waveform fidelity beyond sample-level error. VAMP-Diff reconstructs sharper physiological waveforms than Gaussian-prior baselines, preserves heart-rate information, and maintains respiratory-rate estimator consistency on held-out test signals. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II provides background on PPG, VAEs, and diffusion models. Section III describes the proposed model and training objective. Section IV defines downstream evaluation tasks, and Section V reports empirical results. Finally, concluding remarks are provided in Section VI . II Background II-A Photoplethysmography Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a non-invasive optical technique that measures pulsatile changes in blood volume in peripheral tissue, producing a periodic waveform that encodes heart rate, respiratory rate, and autonomic activity [ 1 , 2 ] . Since PPG sensors are inexpensive and easy to deploy, they are widely used in clinical monitors and wearable devices, with applications that range from cardiovascular monitoring to biometric analysis [ 25 , 26 ] . However, PPG waveforms are difficult to model since clinically relevant information is distributed across peak timing, systolic upstroke, dicrotic morphology, amplitude changes, and slower respiratory variation across the window. Large labeled PPG datasets are also hard to obtain because data collection often requires controlled acquisition, expert annotation, and privacy protection under regulations such as HIPAA, which leaves only a small number of public datasets such as CapnoBase and related physiological signal resources [ 24 , 27 , 25 , 26 ] . II-B Variational Autoencoders and VampPrior Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) [ 17 ] learn an encoder q ϕ ​ ( z ∣ x 0 ) q_{\phi}(z\mid x_{0}) , a decoder p θ ​ ( x 0 ∣ z ) p_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid z) , and a prior p ⁡ ( z ) p(z) through the evidence lower bound [ 28 ] ℒ VAE = 𝔼 q ϕ ​ ( z ∣ x 0 ) [ log p θ ( x 0 ∣ z ) ] − D KL ( q ϕ ( z ∣ x 0 ) ∥ p ( z ) ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VAE}}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z\mid x_{0})}\!\left[\log p_{\theta}(x_{0}\mid z)\right]-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_{\phi}(z\mid x_{0})\,\|\,p(z)\right). (1) The reconstruction loss trains the decoder to recover x 0 x_{0} from the latent variable, and the KL penalty regularizes the encoder posterior against the generation prior. A vanilla VAE usually assumes a fixed prior p ⁡ ( z ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) p(z)=\mathcal{N}(0,I) , which can poorly match the aggregate posterior when the data lies on a structured or curved latent manifold. This mismatch can degrade generation, since samples from 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) may fall outside the latent regions that guide decoder training. The VampPrior [ 22 ] addresses this mismatch by defining the prior as a mixture of encoder posteriors evaluated at K K learnable pseudo-inputs { u k } k = 1 K \{u_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} , p ψ ​ ( z ) = 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K q ϕ ​ ( z ∣ u k ) . p_{\psi}(z)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{\phi}(z\mid u_{k}). (3) The compact VampPrior regularizer in Section III-A builds on this prior and applies the KL to a pooled temporal latent. II-C Denoising Diffusion Models Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) [ 10 ] generate data by learning to reverse a gradual Gaussian noising process. Starting from a clean signal x 0 x_{0} , the forward process samples q ( x t ∣ x 0 ) = 𝒩 ( x t ; α ¯ t x 0 , ( 1 − α ¯ t ) I ) , t = 1 , … , T , q(x_{t}\mid x_{0})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(x_{t};\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,x_{0},(1-\bar{\alpha}_{t})I\right),\qquad t=1,\ldots,T, (4) where α ¯ t \bar{\alpha}_{t} is the cumulative noise schedule. A neural network, often a U-Net architecture [ 29 ] , is trained to recover the clean signal or the injected noise from x t x_{t} . In this paper, our decoder uses the clean-signal prediction parameterization x ^ 0 \widehat{x}_{0} , since the losses in Section III-D act directly on the reconstructed waveform. Sampling from a diffusion model can require many reverse steps, so DDIM [ 30 ] is used at inference to obtain a deterministic and faster reverse trajectory. III VAMP-Diff: VampPrior Latent Diffusion for PPG III-A Temporal Latent Encoder and Prior Regularization The encoder maps each PPG window x 0 ∈ ℝ L x_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{L} to a diagonal Gaussian posterior over a temporal latent sequence, q ϕ ​ ( z ∣ x 0 ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( z , μ ϕ ​ ( x 0 ) , diag ⁡ ( σ ϕ 2 ​ ( x 0 ) ) ) , z ∈ ℝ C z × T z . q_{\phi}(z\mid x_{0})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(z;\mu_{\phi}(x_{0}),\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{\phi}^{2}(x_{0}))\right),\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{z}\times T_{z}}. (5) The sequence structure of z z is retained so that the decoder receives temporally ordered information across the PPG window. A single pooled code can remove the temporal ordering before the denoising decoder receives the latent representation. For unconditional generation, the standard Gaussian prior p ⁡ ( z ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) p(z)=\mathcal{N}(0,I) does not match the aggregate posterior learned by the encoder, thus the VAMP-Diff employs the VampPrior ( 2 ). VampPrior is built from K K learnable pseudo-inputs { u k } k = 1 K \{u_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} , each passed through the same encoder q ϕ ​ ( z ∣ x 0 ) q_{\phi}(z\mid x_{0}) . The pseudo-input initialization samples real training windows under heart-rate and amplitude stratification, as random pseudo-input initialization may lead to an unstable KL behavior early in training. Since z ∈ ℝ C z × T z z\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{z}\times T_{z}} is high-dimensional, we evaluate the VampPrior KL in a pooled latent space. Let A : ℝ C z × T z → ℝ C z × T c , T c < T z , A:\mathbb{R}^{C_{z}\times T_{z}}\to\mathbb{R}^{C_{z}\times T_{c}},\qquad T_{c}<T_{z}, denote temporal pooling, and define z ~ = A ​ z \widetilde{z}=Az . During training, the compact posterior q ϕ A ​ ( z ~ ∣ x 0 ) = A # ​ q ϕ ​ ( z ∣ x 0 ) q_{\phi}^{A}(\widetilde{z}\mid x_{0})=A_{\#}q_{\phi}(z\mid x_{0}) is matched to the compact VampPrior p ψ A ​ ( z ~ ) p_{\psi}^{A}(\widetilde{z}) . IV Downstream Tasks We evaluate downstream behavior using reconstructed test signals to determine whether the learned latent representation preserves physiological content from the original PPG window. For each test signal x 0 x_{0} , the encoder produces z = μ ϕ ​ ( x 0 ) z=\mu_{\phi}(x_{0}) , and the decoder reconstructs x ^ 0 \widehat{x}_{0} through deterministic DDIM with η = 0 \eta=0 , as described in Section III-B . Both x 0 x_{0} and x ^ 0 \widehat{x}_{0} are denormalized with the training-set statistics μ train \mu_{\mathrm{train}} and σ train \sigma_{\mathrm{train}} . This process evaluates the encoder and decoder jointly, since the latent must keep a physiologically relevant structure and the diffusion decoder must recover that structure through the denoising process. We consider three test-split evaluations, heart-rate estimation, respiratory-rate estimator consistency, and reconstruction-based waveform corruption detection. IV-A Heart-Rate Estimation Heart rate (HR) estimation is the first physiological test for PPG, as cardiac rhythm is the dominant periodic component of clean PPG, and accurate recovery depends primarily on inter-beat timing rather than pointwise waveform similarity [ 2 , 3 ] . For each test window, both x 0 x_{0} and x ^ 0 \widehat{x}_{0} are bandpass-filtered to 0.7 0.7 – 3.0 3.0 Hz before cardiac feature extraction. Systolic peaks are detected with minimum inter-peak distance 0.35 0.35 s, prominence 0.1 ​ σ 0.1\sigma of the filtered signal, and height at the 60 60 th percentile. Per-window HR is computed as 60 / IBI ¯ 60/\bar{\mathrm{IBI}} , where IBI ¯ \bar{\mathrm{IBI}} is the mean inter-beat interval. Signal-level reconstruction is evaluated using MAE, RMSE, and Pearson correlation. Cardiac timing fidelity is assessed through HR absolute error and IBI mean absolute error on the VAMP-Diff model. IV-B Respiratory Rate Estimation Respiratory rate (RR) is a more demanding physiological test, since respiration affects PPG through baseline variation, amplitude modulation, and frequency modulation in the 0.1 0.1 – 0.5 0.5 Hz band [ 3 ] . We use a frozen-estimator procedure so that RR evaluation stays independent of VAMP-Diff training. A one-dimensional ResNet is trained once on real PPG to regress RR from CO 2 -derived labels, and the generative model is not used during estimator training. The estimator uses a stride-2 stem with kernel size 11 11 and 32 32 channels, followed by four residual stages with channel widths { 32 , 64 , 128 , 128 } \{32,64,128,128\} , dilation rates { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \{1,2,4,8\} , global average pooling, and a two-layer MLP regression head. Ground-truth RR is obtained from the synchronous EtCO 2 channel in CapnoBase [ 24 ] by peak detection on a five-sample-smoothed signal, with minimum inter-peak distance 1 1 s and prominence 0.05 0.05 . Recordings outside [ 6 , 35 ] [6,35] breaths per minute are excluded. We apply the frozen estimator to real and reconstructed PPG windows, and use MAE recon − MAE real \mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{recon}}-\mathrm{MAE}_{\mathrm{real}} to measure how much RR-relevant information changes after reconstruction. V Empirical Results The proposed VAMP-Diff model is evaluated along two axes: generative quality and reconstruction fidelity, validated through model comparison and downstream physiological inference tasks. The former tests whether the model produces PPG signals that are statistically and morphologically consistent with real data; the latter tests whether the encoded latent z z carries sufficient physiological information to recover clinically meaningful quantities through the decode pipeline, as measured by the downstream tasks of Section IV . V-A Dataset and Preprocessing Experiments use the CapnoBase dataset [ 24 ] , a freely available ICU recording containing PPG and capnography signals from 42 patients, each recorded for approximately 8 minutes at 300 Hz. The PPG channel ( pleth_y ) provides the input signal. Respiratory-rate ground truth is derived from the synchronous EtCO 2 channel ( CO 2 _y ) as described in Section IV-B . Each recording is segmented into overlapping windows of 3,072 3{,}072 samples ( 10.24 10.24 s). A bandpass filter ( 0.7 0.7 – 3.0 3.0 Hz) is applied transiently for peak-based quality checking only; windows with fewer than two detected systolic peaks are discarded. The stored windows retain the full signal spectrum, including the respiratory modulation band ( 0.1 0.1 – 0.5 0.5 Hz), which is necessary for downstream respiratory rate estimation. Windows are normalized using the training-set mean μ train \mu_{\text{train}} and the standard deviation σ train \sigma_{\text{train}} , retained for denormalization at evaluation. The dataset yields 6,815 6{,}815 training, 1,410 1{,}410 validation, and 1,645 1{,}645 test windows. Recordings are split at the patient level, ensuring that no patient appears in more than one split and preventing data leakage between training and evaluation. Removing auxiliary losses causes generation failure, indicating that morphological supervision is necessary for the decoder to produce physiologically valid signals. Random pseudo-input initialization degrades both reconstruction and generation.
